rv.q: “Trash” ultimately feels very inside the box, constrained perhaps by expectations of what Deaf theater aiming for a mainstream stage ought to be.
Trash is a most exceptional and memorable play.

Equally humorous and thoughtful, Trash is a fascinating look into the lives of Deaf men in 21st century America, where anxiety around sex, work, and a creeping sense of obsolesce is aggravated by the daily struggle of existing in a world that has been primarily designed for the hearing majority.
This roommate comedy, performed mostly in American Sign Language, transcends language to communicate universal truths.
If “Trash” is eye-opening for hearing audiences, it is also likely one of the few entertainments that Deaf people can enjoy without compromise.
The engaging Trash embellishes a common New York story of two roommates in conflict by adding an important twist, as well as a variety of theatrical tricks, including audience participation.

cn.t: Critics praise "Trash" for its groundbreaking use of American Sign Language and ingenious theatrical devices that make the Deaf roommates' story accessible to hearing audiences, delivering an engaging and revealing window into Deaf culture.
